analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects about 13 million acres of Alaska's two largest national forests from logging, roads, and mining.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 93 cosponsors — 90 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 independent — but never received a hearing or vote, sitting in the House Resources Committee and its Forests Subcommittee from March 2005 until that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently protected roughly 13 million acres of the Chugach and Tongass National Forests in Alaska, the latter being the largest national forest in the United States. It would have designated about 6.9 million acres as wilderness, another 5.8 million acres as a strict conservation category, and dozens of rivers as wild and scenic, with smaller areas set aside for restoration and low-impact community use. Logging, new road construction, and mining and mineral leasing would be barred in the protected areas, while hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, and Alaska Native and rural subsistence uses would be guaranteed to continue. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who owns these lands in common: hunters, anglers, hikers, and campers would keep guaranteed access to protected forest; Alaska Native and rural residents would keep a legal basis for a subsistence way of life; and salmon runs, which depend on unlogged watersheds and intact stream banks, would be shielded from clearcutting and new roads. Because wilderness and conservation designations are permanent, future generations would inherit the same guarantees rather than having to win them again.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, subsistence users, forest visitors

how_it_helps.text: Would have designated about 6.9 million acres of new wilderness — roughly 3.66 million in the Chugach and 3.23 million in the Tongass — protecting them permanently from logging, road-building, and development while keeping hunting, fishing, hiking, and camping open.
Would have added about 5.8 million acres of Tongass land to the strict Land Use Designation II conservation category and 236,000 acres to wilderness study for possible future protection.
Would have closed and rehabilitated roads and restored logged land and damaged stream banks across about 29,000 acres of restoration areas.
Would have created about 43,100 acres of special management areas that bar clearcutting and new roads while allowing small-scale, community-based use of renewable resources.
Would have designated or studied dozens of rivers as wild, scenic, or recreational, and withdrawn a mile on each side of designated rivers from mining and mineral leasing to protect water quality.
Would have guaranteed continued hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, and Alaska Native and rural subsistence uses, and left state authority over fish and wildlife untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies would lose access to millions of acres of public forest they currently log, and mining and oil, gas, and geothermal developers could no longer stake new claims or leases in protected zones. Some Southeast Alaska towns built around logging would bear job losses, and the Forest Service would take on the cost of closing and rehabilitating old logging roads and managing the new protected areas permanently.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tongass timber operators and mining claimants

drawbacks.text: Barring logging and road construction across most of two giant national forests would sharply cut the commercial timber supply and could cost jobs in Southeast Alaska communities built around the industry; the bill's only continued-use carve-out is small-scale community management in about 43,100 acres of special areas.

Withdrawing the protected lands from mining, mineral, and geothermal leasing would foreclose future mineral and energy development on those federal acres, though existing valid rights would be honored.
Wilderness and conservation designations are effectively permanent, so a future Congress could not easily return the land to timber or mineral production if conditions changed.
The Forest Service would bear new costs to close and rehabilitate roads, prepare maps and management plans, and manage the new areas indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is permanent on both sides. The public would give up commercial logging and new mineral development on roughly 13 million acres of federal land it owns, and some timber-dependent Southeast Alaska towns would bear real job losses the bill does little to offset. In return, hunting, fishing, subsistence, and recreation would be guaranteed in perpetuity, damaged roads and streams would be restored, and no future Congress could quietly reverse the arrangement. How one weighs this depends on how much weight goes to intact forest, salmon rivers, and guaranteed public access versus timber supply and resource development; the bill allowed only small community-scale carve-outs for continued local use.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Resources Committee, which sent it to its Forests and Forest Health Subcommittee two days later; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 8, 2005 with 75 original cosponsors named in the bill text.
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources the same day, and on March 11, 2005 to that committee's Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill finished with 93 cosponsors: 90 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 independent.
It would have designated about 3.66 million acres of the Chugach and 3.23 million acres of the Tongass as wilderness.
It would have added about 5.79 million acres of Tongass land to the Land Use Designation II conservation category and 236,000 acres to wilderness study.
Protected lands and a one-mile band along newly designated rivers would have been withdrawn from mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, subject to valid existing rights.
About 29,000 acres of logged and road-damaged land would have been designated for restoration, with roads closed and rehabilitated to a natural condition.
About 43,100 acres would have become special management areas where clearcutting and most new roads are barred but small-scale community use is allowed.

The bill declared it Congress's intent to safeguard these lands permanently, guarantee public hunting, fishing, hiking, and camping, and continue the opportunity for Alaskans to live a subsistence way of life.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber and mining interests came out ahead: with no law change, the lands stayed open to logging, road-building, and mineral claims for another two-year Congress, and no one ever had to vote on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber and mining interests kept access

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Alaska Rainforest Conservation Act on March 8, 2005 with 75 original cosponsors.

for.name: National conservation groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for permanent protection of the Tongass and Chugach and supported the bill.

against.name: Rep. Richard Pombo
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; it was sent to the Forests and Forest Health Subcommittee on March 11, 2005, and no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Southeast Alaska timber industry
against.role: Logging companies and trade groups dependent on Tongass timber sales
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanding wilderness and roadless protections in the Tongass, which would shrink the commercial timber base available for logging.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship ran 90 Democrats to 2 Republicans and 1 independent, and the Republican-led Resources Committee never scheduled the bill for any action.

industries.industry: Logging and timber (Tongass and Chugach operators)
industries.note: The bill would bar logging and new road-building across about 6.9 million acres of new wilderness and 5.8 million acres of conservation land in the two forests, and prohibit clearcutting in special management areas. Commercial operators would lose most of the public land base they log; ordinary people would gain the protected forest in its place.

industries.industry: Mining, oil, gas, and geothermal developers
industries.note: Designated lands would be withdrawn from staking and patenting under the mining laws and from mineral and geothermal leasing, closing them to new claims and leases, subject to valid existing rights; a one-mile band along newly designated rivers would also be withdrawn.

industries.industry: Alaska fishing, guiding, and tourism businesses
industries.note: The bill keeps hunting, fishing, hiking, and camping open and restores logged and road-damaged lands and stream banks, protecting the salmon habitat and scenery that sport and commercial fishing and nature tourism depend on.
